cl_ket_near_death.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
cl_ket_near_death.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.
cl_ket_near_death.rate: One study comparing words in reports people chose to post online with near-death accounts written years later. Nobody checked the drugs, and ketamine's lead over LSD was small.
cl_ket_near_death.note: Short now answers first; How adds the 4-in-5 settings, accounts after anaesthesia or drugs, and the summary's overreach.

cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.q: What side effects does MDMA cause in therapy trials?
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.rate: Reviews pooling 8 trials with 298 people, mostly PTSD trials from one sponsor. Staff noting side effects probably knew who got MDMA, and few trials looked beyond PTSD.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.note: Plainer question; short leads with effects, says short-lived not 'gone within a week'; shorter sentences; adds 4 of 13.

cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.short: Tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, two reviews say. So the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.but: The reviews give no numbers. Not how long a break must be, or how much the risk of a fatal overdose rises.
how: The older review offers this as a possible explanation. It says tolerance may fade quickly, and not at the same pace for every effect. But there's little data on how fast.
The idea rests on one hair study. People who died of heroin overdose had less morphine in their hair than people still using. The review reads that as less use before death.
The newer review gives prison and detox as examples of a break; the older one, which it cites, doesn't.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.rate: It's second-hand: two reviews, one citing the other, describe a few older studies that weren't checked here. Neither gives any numbers.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.note: Short answers the why first; How says what the hair study found; rate kept to what the claim says.

cl_ket_music.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
cl_ket_music.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.
cl_ket_music.rate: One trial of 32 patients, reporting only blood pressure. The earlier studies are small, mostly during medical procedures, and known only through a review.
cl_ket_music.note: Short opens with nobody knows; drops hospital, children and surgery (not in claim); adds what people in interviews said.

cl_lsd_emergency.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
cl_lsd_emergency.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.
cl_lsd_emergency.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or whether the drug was really LSD, and people who could not answer are missing.

freq.what: people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 102 of 10,293 for LSD and 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms, all self-reported.

cl_lsd_emergency.note: But split for reading level; How says symptoms were ticked, not checked, and adds the 40 who took longer.

cl_can_secondhand_test.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
cl_can_secondhand_test.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once, and for 3 to 7, a lab check would have confirmed it.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.
cl_can_secondhand_test.rate: One lab experiment: 18 people, 6 in each of three settings, sat beside people smoking in a sealed room, in thick smoke in two of them. Everyday exposure was not tested.
cl_can_secondhand_test.note: Smoke was thick in only two of three sessions, so smoky room; How now shows the 12 behind the short.

cl_dc_benzo_strips.q: Do benzo test strips catch etizolam and other newer benzos?
cl_dc_benzo_strips.short: Not reliably. At one drug-checking service, strips caught newer benzos in 15 of 24 samples that had them, and just 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.
cl_dc_benzo_strips.but: A lab checked only some samples, not picked at random. Some were chosen because of a suspected benzo overdose.
how: At eight health sites, samples were tested with strips, and a lab checked some of them.
Strips caught 7 of 8 samples with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam. With etizolam alone, they caught only 8 of 16.
They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which the lab found none; what set those off wasn't reported.
The same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam, even at 40 or more times the level at which it caught other benzos. An earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up.
cl_dc_benzo_strips.rate: One brand of urine strip, tried at one Canadian drug-checking programme and on pure samples in a lab. Only 159 of 1368 samples were lab-checked, and those were not picked at random.

freq.what: samples with a newer benzodiazepine showed it on the strip
freq.note: 15 of 24 samples at one drug-checking service, 2018 to 2020. With etizolam alone, 8 of 16.

cl_dc_benzo_strips.note: People's words; Not reliably fits 15 of 24 (the freq); How adds 7 of 8 and the 40-times lab result.

cl_dc_xylazine_strips.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
cl_dc_xylazine_strips.but: One batch of strips was read in a lab. The samples were residues from used equipment, not powders.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.
cl_dc_xylazine_strips.rate: Two lab studies by one team. The 97-in-100 figure leaves out samples with only a little xylazine, and no one tried the strips on street powders or pills, or outside a lab.

freq.title: Out of every 100 samples with xylazine, how many read positive?
pairs: samples with at least the amount the strip is made to find
freq.note: 37 of 38 and 6 of 28 residue samples, one batch of strips, read in a lab.

cl_dc_xylazine_strips.note: Short opens with a conditional yes and adds 6 of 28 (the freq); rate kept to the claim.

cl_mdma_indications_overview.q: Can MDMA therapy help with anything besides PTSD?
cl_mdma_indications_overview.short: Nobody can say yet. Outside PTSD, it's been tried for a few things. They include tinnitus, drinking problems, and anxiety in autistic adults or in people who are very ill.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.but: Each had one tiny trial at most, the biggest with 18 people. And people could usually tell if they'd had MDMA.
how: Reviews up to 2024 found one trial each. There were 18 people anxious about a serious illness, 12 autistic adults with social anxiety, and 13 people with tinnitus.
A study of 14 people with alcohol problems, and one of 6 couples, had no comparison group.
In the serious-illness trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA, but the trial was too small to be sure.
A critical review found only the two later PTSD trials were randomized with over 15 people per group. It called even those results a signal needing repeating.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.rate: Each condition rests on one tiny trial at most, the largest with 18 people. People could usually tell whether they'd had MDMA, and comparisons didn't run for long.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.note: Question as people ask it; short answers and names what was tried; rate drops self-rating (not in claim).

cl_psi_addiction.short: Maybe. In one trial, people given psilocybin with talk therapy drank heavily on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 with a comparison pill.
cl_psi_addiction.but: Almost everyone could tell if they got psilocybin, and people reported their own drinking.
how: At 2 US universities, 93 adults dependent on alcohol were offered 12 talk-therapy sessions. Chance decided who also got psilocybin twice or a comparison pill.
Heavy drinking had already more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of therapy. That was before any psilocybin or comparison pill.
After about 94 in 100 sessions, people guessed right whether they had psilocybin. So what they expected may explain part of the gap.
cl_psi_addiction.rate: One trial of 93 adults with drinking problems: almost everyone could tell whether they got psilocybin, and they reported their own drinking. It was too small to be sure how big the difference is.

freq.title: Out of every 100 days in the 8 months after the first dose, how many were heavy-drinking days?
pairs: days for people given psilocybin with talk therapy
days for people given a comparison pill with the same therapy
freq.note: One trial of 93 adults with alcohol use disorder at two US universities: 9.7 against 23.6 in 100 days, as people reported them. Heavy drinking had more than halved in both groups before any pill.

cl_psi_addiction.note: Already direct and plain, with the freq numbers in the short; kept unchanged.

cl_gen_antidrug_ads.short: No sign they did. Congress put nearly $1 billion into the campaign, but teen cannabis use stayed flat, and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens had ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.rate: One national survey followed US teens from 1999 to 2004. Almost every teen saw the ads, so no group without them could be compared, and teens reported their own ad viewing and cannabis use.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.note: Already direct, blunt and plain; one How sentence split for reading level, otherwise unchanged.

cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.short: Yes, some do. People judged a person more harshly when their troubles were said to come from drug use, not a health concern.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.but: People rated made-up stories. No one checked how people are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, couldn't take part.
When Alex's trouble was put down to drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted much more distance and saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money game, they took slightly more from Alex.
Calling it a brain disease instead of a problem made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested labels on about 500 mental health workers. Calling a man a substance abuser, not someone with a substance use disorder, got slightly more blame and punishment. It's a shaky result.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.rate: A fair test: chance decided which story each of 1,613 online volunteers read. But readers gave their views after one made-up story, and many were young.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.note: Short answers first; quote marks dropped; How points trimmed; rate drops a reason not in the claim.

cl_gen_remission.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated. In a US survey, 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent about 3 years later.
cl_gen_remission.but: How many depends on who is counted. Recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers back from Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics there, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.
In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some still had a few.

Across 21 studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, depending on how deaths and dropouts are counted. For many, the authors say, the problem is long-lasting.

For alcohol, figures for recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, because studies count different groups. Many who recovered were never treated. Far fewer of everyone with a problem recover untreated in a year.
cl_gen_remission.rate: Interviews with soldiers back from Vietnam and a US national survey, plus reviews. Figures on recovery without treatment come second-hand from a review that did not check how good its 27 studies were.

freq.what: adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent about 3 years later
freq.note: US national survey, 2001–2002 and 2004–2005; some still had one or two signs; the editors’ count from the study’s numbers, not weighted, so not a national estimate.

cl_gen_remission.note: Short carries the freq's 64 in 100; How drops 17 years (pooled figures fit no time point); sentences split.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.but: These only count people who got ill. So they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, so drinking more than it needs waters down the salt. The UK authors say how it happens is not yet known.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.rate: Records from two poison services, in the UK and California, which agree. But MDMA was confirmed by tests in only some cases, and in California only about a third had blood salt measured.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.note: Short answers the water question first; But adds that amounts were never compared; tablet counts dropped.
